deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of Riemann's 'Mechanik des Ohres' (published posthumously by Henle, 1867). On the previous page Riemann estimates the dynamic range of hearing. He cites Nicholson's report that the sentries' calls at Portsmouth are heard at Ryde, 4–5 English miles away. He takes the power of sound to fall off with the inverse square of distance. Since 4–5 miles is more than 2000 times 8–10 ft, the mechanical power is about a 'million' times smaller (strictly about 4 million), and the amplitudes are about 2000 times smaller. He then appeals to the newer work on how estimated loudness relates to mechanical intensity (Fechner) and to the stellar-magnitude analogy: brightness magnitude rises arithmetically while mechanical power falls geometrically.

This page:

(1) Magnitude scale for sounds. Divide sounds, from ordinary loudness down to the barely audible, into classes ('Größen') 1 to 8. The image reads 'achten', not 'sechsten'. Assign mechanical power P_n = 10^{-(n-1)} P_1. So P_2 = P_1/10, P_3 = P_1/100, ..., P_8 = 10^{-7} P_1 ('den zehn Millionten Theil').

(2) Amplitudes. Implicitly (my gloss), at fixed frequency the power is proportional to the square of the amplitude A. Hence A_n = 10^{-(n-1)/2} A_1. This gives A_1 : A_3 : A_5 : A_7 = 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000, as written. In modern terms this is a logarithmic intensity scale with exactly one bel (10 dB) per step, covering 70 dB.

(3) Physiological argument. Some authors assume the strength of loud sounds is reduced at the eardrum (by tensing the tympanic membrane, tensor tympani). Riemann calls this an untenable conjecture. Protective devices may act against a violent bang that threatens the labyrinth. But he sees no analogue of the eye's light-adaptation (pupil) in the ear, which would also be harmful for exact perception of music.

(4) Consequence. There is no reason to assume a different ratio between air motion, eardrum motion and stapes-footplate motion for distant sounds (about 20,000 ft) than for near ones. Suppose the stapes motion at 10 ft were just at the threshold of microscopic visibility. Then for a source at 20,000 ft (a 2000-fold increase in distance) the motions would be 2000 times smaller. They would therefore need a further 2000-fold magnification to be just perceptible. So the ear responds to sub-microscopic displacements.

(5) Section II: design requirements. For the middle-ear apparatus to transmit such tiny motions:
- the conducting parts (ossicles) must fit exactly against each other where they touch;
- at those points their contact must be closed, not merely 'nearly' (to within less than the amplitude of motion);
- only a small part of the mechanical energy may be lost to other work, such as stretching joint capsules and membranes.

The page ends by turning to the elastic rim of the membrane of the oval window around the stapes footplate. This continues on the next page: the rim must be compliant, otherwise it would absorb the footplate's vibrations.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The amplitude ratios 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000 for magnitudes 1, 3, 5, 7 follow correctly from a power ratio of 10 per magnitude together with power proportional to amplitude squared. The latter assumption is implicit.

Carried over from the previous page: a distance ratio of 2000 under the inverse-square law gives a power ratio of 4×10^6, not 10^6 ('eine Million'). This is a loose order-of-magnitude rounding; the amplitude ratio of 2000 is stated correctly.
The factor of 10 per 'magnitude' is arbitrary and does not match Pogson's stellar ratio (about 2.512 per magnitude). Riemann presents it only as an analogy, so it is not strictly an error.

Physiologically, the claim that there is no attenuating mechanism is now partly superseded: the acoustic (stapedius/tensor tympani) reflex does attenuate loud sounds. Riemann allows protective mechanisms only for violent bangs.

results.what: Logarithmic magnitude scale for sound intensity, with a factor of 10 in power per step, modelled on stellar magnitudes; dynamic range of hearing about 10^7 in power.
results.modern_name: Logarithmic intensity level (bel/decibel scale); Weber–Fechner law applied to loudness
results.usually_credited_to: Fechner (1860) for the psychophysical log law; Pogson (1856) for stellar magnitudes; the bel/decibel as a unit is from Bell Labs (1920s)

results.what: Amplitude scales as the square root of power, so two magnitude steps give a factor of 10 in amplitude.
Inverse-square estimate showing that eardrum/stapes motions for faint audible sounds are sub-microscopic (about 2000 times smaller than at 10 ft for a source 20,000 ft away).
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1866/67); later quantitative work by Rayleigh, Wien, Békésy

results.what: Design requirements for the ossicular chain: exact contact at the joints and minimal energy loss to capsules and membranes; argument against tympanic-membrane gain control.
results.modern_name: Middle-ear impedance transformer / ossicular coupling efficiency

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of Riemann's published 'Mechanik des Ohres', which Henle edited in 1867 and which includes the Portsmouth example and the Fechner/stellar-magnitude analogy. The factor-10-per-step scale is effectively a bel scale, which is a pleasant anticipation of decibel notation. But it is a direct application of Fechner/Pogson-style logarithmic scaling, not a new result.

checkable.asserts: The power of an eighth-magnitude sound is one ten-millionth of a first-magnitude sound.

checkable.sympy: [sqrt(Rational(1,10)**(n-1)) for n in [1,3,5,7]] == [1, Rational(1,10), Rational(1,100), Rational(1,1000)]
checkable.asserts: The amplitude ratios for magnitudes 1, 3, 5, 7 are 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000.
A distance ratio of 2000 under the inverse-square law gives a power ratio of 4·10^6 (the text loosely says 'a million').
The amplitude ratio equals the distance ratio of 2000.
4.5 English miles is more than 2000 times 10 ft.

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the image reads 'von der ersten bis zur achten Größe', not 'sechsten'. This matches the 10^-7 = 1/10,000,000 figure for the last class.
Line 4: 'für die achte 1/10,000000', not 'sechste'. Ten million (10^-7) requires the eighth magnitude at a factor of 10 per step.

Line 1: the interlinear insertion 'dann zwischen' probably reads 'Theilt man die Schalle' or 'Theilen wir'; the opening is 'Theilt man ... die Schalle von denen gewöhnlicher Stärke bis zu dem eben noch wahrnehmbaren in Schalle...' (uncertain).

Line 'Ich habe aber bei der Betrachtung...': most likely 'Ich habe ... beim Trommelfell Halt gemacht, weil Einige eine Abschwächung des stärkeren Schalls (durch Spannung des Trommelfells?) annehmen'. The word read as 'Änderung' is more likely 'Abschwächung'/'Dämpfung'.
The line read as 'Beleuchtungs-... Gesichtsfeld' is likely 'Beleuchtungsgrad des Gesichtsfeldes ... Pupille ... Auge'. The analogy is to pupil light-adaptation (uncertain).
The left-margin insertion 'nicht weniger beträchtlich' is likely 'nicht hinreichend deutlich' or similar (uncertain).
